The jurisdiction is a US state (anonymised) — but must not identify. Rate on facts.

Key traveler-facing exposures:

National parent regime: passport/visa sex-marker restrictions, X markers stopped for new issues, border officers instructed to refuse cases with document discrepancies and consider lifetime fraud ineligibility for suspected misrepresentation of sex; trans athletes banned; advisories from foreign governments; detention/custody harms (conversion-therapy-like practices in national prisons, immigration custody abuse); counterterrorism rhetoric listing "radically pro-transgender" groups.

These are traveler-facing: border document mismatch → refusal, potential permanent ineligibility finding. That's a serious universal-exposure for a trans traveler whose documents don't match appearance.

Division layer: state anti-discrimination law covering gender identity in public accommodations, employment, housing; hate crime enhancements for gender identity since 2019; gay/trans panic defence abolished; enforcement documented (July 2026 civil rights ruling for striking a trans woman). But: birth certificate change requires surgery; 2024/2025 bans on gender-affirming care for minors; sports ban; 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents (raw count, no denominator — rule 16/17 says raw counts without denominators carry no magnitude); description as "least safe state in the region for trans citizens" — attributed, resident-facing.

For a visitor: the national border regime is the biggest traveler-facing exposure. Passport marked with gender; border officers instructed to refuse where reasonable doubt on applicant's sex; possible fraud finding with lifetime ineligibility. That's a tier-1 universal exposure for the outable traveler — document/ID-examination mismatch. Also facilities bans: national bar on trans people in government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with gender identity — that applies to visitors in government buildings. And 9 states ban facilities in all government buildings; is this state among them? Not stated. Division evidence doesn't say this state has a bathroom ban. So we shouldn't attribute a bathroom ban to this state. Facilities in this state: not stated as banned.

So the traveler-facing worst features: national border/document regime (universal exposure, refusal/stranding, potential lifetime fraud finding), plus national facility exclusion in government-funded buildings, plus national-level hostile framing. Division adds functioning anti-discrimination law, hate-crime coverage, enforced civil rights statute, but also care bans (resident-facing for minors — not visitor) and hostile climate (attributed "least safe").

Rules: parental regime attaches to this dossier. So the national regime applies and weighs heavily. Also liability clause: functioning courts are not mitigation when institutions enforce a hostile rule — but here courts also enforce protections for trans people (civil rights statute enforced against an attacker). Both.

Where does this sit? Compare to anchors: 0.35 examples have universal institutional exposure (facility exclusion, custody, police extortion) with inadequate remedy. 0.45 similar with universal-exposure practice. 0.55 repeated visitor-facing harms with partial remedy.

Here: national border screening can refuse entry for document mismatch and potentially lifetime ineligibility — severe (denial of entry/stranding, level 3-4). PLUS facility exclusion in federal buildings — universal exposure. PLUS custody harms documented (immigration custody, forced labour, sexual abuse for trans detainees) — catastrophic severity if detained, though probability unknown. But on the other side: division-level enforced anti-discrimination protections, hate crime law, 88% public support for protections, hate crime enhancements, trans panic defence abolished. Social acceptance: 88% support discrimination protections — that's a positive. But the national poll says 66% support assigned sex at birth on documents.

The rubric says state-imposed universal exposure with no working remedy is tier 1. Border document regime is tier 1 for the outable traveler. Effective remedy? The passport suit is in litigation; no remedy shown working. So tier 1 remains.

Social/civil rights layer at division level mitigates: hotels, accommodations, enforcement, prosecutions. That's tier 5-ish positives.

Net: I'd put this around 0.40–0.45. Universal exposure at the border (denial of entry, potential lifetime fraud finding) is a serious, unavoidable, traveler-facing measure; the state layer provides genuine working protections in everyday services. Compare 0.45-A (national birth-sex bathroom rule enforced, no remedy, but polite public) → 0.45. Here the border regime is arguably worse than a bathroom rule in severity (denial of entry, stranding, lifetime ineligibility) though it triggers only on suspicion/discrepancy — but every trans traveler passes through the border. Meanwhile the division's service protections are strong.

However there's also the custody documented abuse — but that's for detainees; probability unknown; still, immigration custody with documented forced labour and sexual abuse of trans men is severe. Tier-1/high.

Also facilities: the national exclusion from government-funded single-sex facilities affects visitors (national buildings, airports?). Actually the executive order barred trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities — that's a universal exposure for visitors entering federal buildings.

I'll go with 0.40. Maybe 0.38. The state layer positives (enforced civil rights statute, hate crime enhancements, 88% support, no state bathroom ban documented) push above 0.35. The national border regime and facility exclusion and custody harms pull below 0.5. I'll say 0.40.
